_doc: Botanicals and other non-nutrient ingredients with safety signals in NIH NCCIH fact sheets ("Herbs at a Glance") and NIH ODS fact sheets. An ingredient is matched when its DSLD ingredient group or name equals one of "match" after normalization and removal of trailing plant-part/preparation words (root, leaf, extract, powder...); never by substring. A botanical's exclude_words (whole words in the label name or group) rule a match out, for example DGL licorice. Signals summarize the cited page; the list is not exhaustive. A signal with "relay": false is listed in botanicals[] but kept out of agent_summary, because the ingredient is common in small amounts (multivitamins) and the signal concerns concentrated or high-dose products; a dose check surfaces it when one applies.

ashwagandha.name: Ashwagandha

signals.summary: NCCIH: although rare, a number of cases link liver injury to ashwagandha supplements.

NCCIH: not recommended for people with thyroid disorders or autoimmune conditions, before surgery, or with hormone-sensitive prostate cancer; long-term safety (beyond about 3 months) is not well established.

ashwagandha.pregnancy: NCCIH: avoid ashwagandha during pregnancy and while breastfeeding.

medications.summary: NCCIH lists possible interactions between ashwagandha and diabetes medications.
NCCIH lists possible interactions between ashwagandha and blood pressure medications.
NCCIH lists possible interactions between ashwagandha and immunosuppressants.
NCCIH lists possible interactions between ashwagandha and sedatives.
NCCIH lists possible interactions between ashwagandha and anti-seizure medications.
NCCIH lists possible interactions between ashwagandha and thyroid hormone medications.

signals.summary: NCCIH: liver injury has been reported, mainly with green tea extract in tablets or capsules, not with green tea as a drink. NIH ODS: USP advises taking extracts with food, because problems are more likely on an empty stomach.

medications.summary: NCCIH: high-dose green tea may lower blood levels of nadolol and reduce its effect.
NCCIH: green tea extract can reduce blood levels of atorvastatin.
NCCIH: an NCCIH-funded study found an interaction between green tea and raloxifene.

dose_checks.summary: In the Minnesota Green Tea Trial, extract with 843 mg EGCG a day for 12 months significantly raised liver enzymes, with moderate or worse abnormalities in some women (NIH ODS).

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Dietary Supplements for Weight Loss

turmeric.name: Turmeric / curcumin

signals.summary: NCCIH: liver damage has been reported with highly bioavailable curcumin products (often combined with piperine from black pepper); stop and see a health care provider with fatigue, nausea, dark urine or jaundice.

turmeric.pregnancy: NCCIH: turmeric supplements may be unsafe during pregnancy; little is known about amounts above food levels while breastfeeding.

st-johns-wort.name: St. John's wort

signals.summary: NCCIH: St. John's wort can weaken the effects of many medicines, including life-saving ones, and with serotonin-affecting drugs may cause serious serotonin-related side effects.
NCCIH: large oral doses may cause severe skin reactions after sun exposure.

st-johns-wort.pregnancy: NCCIH: may be unsafe in pregnancy (possible birth defects); breastfed infants may develop colic, drowsiness and lethargy.

medications.summary: NCCIH: St. John's wort can weaken the effect of this medicine (NIH names it among the drugs affected).
NCCIH: St. John's wort can weaken the effect of birth control pills.
NCCIH: combined with antidepressants or other serotonin-affecting drugs, St. John's wort may cause serious serotonin-related side effects.

ginkgo.name: Ginkgo

signals.summary: NCCIH: ginkgo may increase the risk of bleeding in people taking anticoagulants such as warfarin.

ginkgo.pregnancy: NCCIH: ginkgo may be unsafe in pregnancy and might cause extra bleeding during delivery; little is known about breastfeeding.

medications.summary: NCCIH: ginkgo may increase the risk of bleeding in people taking anticoagulants such as warfarin.

kava.name: Kava

signals.summary: NCCIH: kava products have been linked to rare cases of liver injury, some serious or fatal.
NCCIH: kava should not be used with alcohol or other sedating substances such as benzodiazepines.

kava.pregnancy: NCCIH: kava may carry special risks during pregnancy or breastfeeding.

medications.summary: NCCIH: kava should not be used together with sedatives such as benzodiazepines.

black-cohosh.name: Black cohosh

signals.summary: NCCIH: rare cases of liver damage, some very serious, have been reported with products labeled as black cohosh (causation uncertain; some products contained the wrong herb). See a provider with dark urine or fatigue.

black-cohosh.pregnancy: NCCIH: black cohosh may be unsafe during pregnancy or while breastfeeding.

garcinia-cambogia.name: Garcinia cambogia

signals.summary: NCCIH: it may be unsafe to consume garcinia cambogia products; several cases of liver damage have been reported, some severe. NIH ODS: 10 reported liver toxicity cases included one death and two transplants (most products also had other ingredients).

garcinia-cambogia.pregnancy: NCCIH: little is known about safety in pregnancy or breastfeeding.

medications.summary: NCCIH: interactions have been reported between garcinia cambogia and drugs that affect serotonin.

red-yeast-rice.name: Red yeast rice

signals.summary: NCCIH: monacolin K in red yeast rice is chemically the same as lovastatin, so products can have statin side effects (muscle, kidney and liver damage) and statin drug interactions; content varies widely and isn't on the label. Some products contain citrinin, a kidney toxin.

red-yeast-rice.pregnancy: NCCIH: not recommended during pregnancy or lactation.

medications.summary: NCCIH: red yeast rice contains monacolin K (identical to lovastatin) and can have the same interactions and side effects as statins; taking it with a statin doubles up.

goldenseal.name: Goldenseal

signals.summary: NCCIH: goldenseal may change how the body processes many medications.

goldenseal.pregnancy: NCCIH: do not use goldenseal when pregnant or breastfeeding or give it to infants; its berberine can be harmful to newborns.

medications.summary: NCCIH: in an NCCIH-funded study, goldenseal lowered metformin levels by about 25%, which could hinder glucose control.

berberine.name: Berberine
berberine.pregnancy: NCCIH (goldenseal fact sheet): berberine can be harmful to newborns; goldenseal, its main source, should not be used in pregnancy or breastfeeding or given to infants.

yohimbe.name: Yohimbe

signals.summary: NCCIH: yohimbine has been associated with irregular heartbeat, blood pressure problems, heart attacks and seizures; yohimbe is restricted or banned in many countries, and labels rarely state the yohimbine content.

yohimbe.pregnancy: NCCIH: oral yohimbe might be unsafe in pregnancy or while breastfeeding.

medications.summary: NCCIH: avoid yohimbe with MAO inhibitors or tricyclic antidepressants.

ephedra.name: Ephedra (ma huang)

signals.summary: NCCIH: FDA banned dietary supplements containing ephedrine alkaloids in 2004; ephedra can be life-threatening or disabling (high blood pressure, heart attack, seizure, stroke, psychosis), even at low doses.

ephedra.pregnancy: NCCIH: unsafe during pregnancy, breastfeeding and for children.

valerian.name: Valerian

signals.summary: NCCIH: valerian should not be taken with alcohol or sedatives; rare liver injury has been reported, mostly with combination products. Studied at 300-600 mg a day for up to 6 weeks; long-term safety is unknown.

valerian.pregnancy: NCCIH: little is known about safety in pregnancy or breastfeeding.

medications.summary: NCCIH: valerian should not be taken along with sedatives.

dose_checks.summary: Above the 300-600 mg a day NCCIH describes for short-term use (up to 6 weeks); long-term safety is unknown.

signals.summary: NCCIH: some people have allergic reactions to echinacea, which may be severe; check with a pediatrician before giving it to a child.

medications.summary: NCCIH: researchers have theoretical concerns about echinacea with immunosuppressants.

garlic.name: Garlic

signals.summary: NCCIH: garlic supplements may increase the risk of bleeding; tell your health care providers, especially before surgery or if you take anticoagulants or aspirin.
NCCIH: side effects include breath and body odor, abdominal pain, gas and nausea; some people are allergic to garlic.

garlic.pregnancy: NCCIH: garlic in amounts larger than those in food may be unsafe during pregnancy or while breastfeeding.

medications.summary: NCCIH: garlic supplements may increase the risk of bleeding; talk with your health care provider before using garlic with an anticoagulant.

asian-ginseng.name: Asian ginseng

signals.summary: NCCIH: Asian ginseng may interfere with blood clotting and may worsen autoimmune disorders.
NCCIH: trouble sleeping is the most common side effect; uncommon reports include severe rash, liver damage and severe allergic reactions.

asian-ginseng.pregnancy: NCCIH: Asian ginseng taken by mouth may be unsafe during pregnancy (a chemical in it caused birth defects in animals); little is known about breastfeeding.

medications.summary: NCCIH: Asian ginseng might lower blood sugar; people with diabetes should consult their health care provider before using it.

saw-palmetto.name: Saw palmetto

signals.summary: NCCIH: side effects are mild and infrequent and may include digestive symptoms, dizziness and headache.

saw-palmetto.pregnancy: NCCIH: saw palmetto may be unsafe during pregnancy or while breastfeeding.

milk-thistle.name: Milk thistle

signals.summary: NCCIH: milk thistle may cause allergic reactions, particularly in people allergic to related plants such as ragweed, chrysanthemum, marigold and daisy.
NCCIH: some products have contained amounts of silymarin very different from the label, or pesticides, microbes or mold toxins.

milk-thistle.pregnancy: NCCIH: little is known about milk thistle's safety during pregnancy or breastfeeding.

licorice-root.name: Licorice root

signals.summary: NCCIH: glycyrrhizin in licorice root can cause irregular heartbeat and cardiac arrest, especially in large amounts or with long-term use. Even small amounts have been linked to severe effects in people with high blood pressure, heart or kidney conditions, or a high-salt diet.

licorice-root.pregnancy: NCCIH: large amounts of licorice (about 250 g a week) during pregnancy are unsafe and can raise the risk of delivery before 38 weeks; little is known about breastfeeding.

medications.summary: NCCIH: interactions between licorice and corticosteroids have been reported.

bitter-orange.name: Bitter orange

signals.summary: NCCIH: serious concerns have been raised about supplements containing bitter orange; abnormal heart rhythms, heart attacks and strokes have been reported, mostly with products that had several ingredients, and studies of its effect on blood pressure and heart rate disagree.

NCCIH: in FDA testing few bitter orange supplements matched the synephrine content on their labels, and some contained synthetic amines that are not legal dietary ingredients; the NCAA lists synephrine (bitter orange) as a banned stimulant.

bitter-orange.pregnancy: NCCIH: bitter orange may be unsafe during pregnancy or while breastfeeding.

fenugreek.name: Fenugreek

signals.summary: NCCIH: fenugreek can cause allergic reactions, including serious reactions, in some people.
NCCIH: side effects include diarrhea, nausea and other digestive symptoms; large doses may cause a harmful drop in blood sugar.

fenugreek.pregnancy: NCCIH: fenugreek in amounts greater than those in food is unsafe during pregnancy and has been linked to birth defects in animals and people; little is known about larger amounts while breastfeeding.

cinnamon.name: Cinnamon

signals.summary: NCCIH: cassia cinnamon, the most common type sold in the US, contains coumarin, which might cause or worsen liver disease; most products don't contain enough to make you sick, but prolonged use or large amounts could be a problem for people with liver disease. Ceylon cinnamon has only traces, and labels often don't say which type was used.
NCCIH: larger amounts or long-term use are sometimes linked to digestive problems or allergic reactions.

cinnamon.pregnancy: NCCIH: Ceylon cinnamon in amounts larger than those in food is considered unsafe during pregnancy; little is known about larger amounts while breastfeeding.

medications.summary: NCCIH (Diabetes and Dietary Supplements): using herbal supplements such as cinnamon with diabetes medicines can cause unwanted side effects; tell your health care provider about any herbal supplements you take.

dose_checks.summary: Above the usual 3-5 g a day maintenance dose; NIH ODS describes 20 g a day only as a 5-7 day loading phase. Weight gain (water retention) is the consistent effect.

source.name: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Dietary Supplements for Exercise and Athletic Performance

dose_checks.summary: Above the highest daily dose in the studies NIH ODS cites (25 g a day for 6-7 days).
